name: Happy Numbers
line: Happy Numbers places with a test, then gives curriculum tasks. In AMP, assessment and teaching happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Happy Numbers: Happy Numbers places with a test, then gives curriculum tasks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Happy Numbers places a student with a separate test, then the student works through curriculum tasks toward goals set in minutes and tasks [6][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Happy Numbers starts with a required placement test: adaptive, multiple choice and untimed, scored on the Quantile scale [6][7]. Benchmark tests check progress during the year [8].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Happy Numbers the unit is the curriculum task, grouped in modules, and some modules open with a pretest or close with an exit ticket [3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [15].

reasons.title: Help is recorded, not forbidden
reasons.body: In AMP, help is in reach at every problem. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. In Happy Numbers' grade 3 tasks, hints come in a task's early levels and not in its later ones [5].

reasons.title: What counts as learned
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Happy Numbers sets its goals in minutes and tasks, and its studies measure use by tasks solved [2][9][10]. We found no published rule for when a skill counts as learned [3][5].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Some Happy Numbers tasks revisit earlier skills [5]. Benchmark tests check progress during the year [8]. We found no scheduled review of learned skills in its published curriculum pages [3][5]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Happy Numbers' placement test sets a starting point on the Quantile scale [6][7]. It covers PreK through grade 5 [1].

rows.start: A required placement test: adaptive, multiple choice and untimed, scored on the Quantile scale [6][7].
rows.teaching: Interactive tasks that move from objects and diagrams to equations, with voice prompts in PreK. Hints in a task's early levels, none in later ones [3][5].
rows.next: Curriculum tasks from the placement starting point [6]. Teachers set time and task targets for each student [2].
rows.mastery: Goals counted in minutes and tasks [2][9]. We found no published rule for when a skill counts as learned [3][5].
rows.review: Some tasks revisit earlier skills, and benchmark tests check progress [5][8]. No scheduled review of learned skills found [3][5].
rows.print: None found in the pages we read [3][5].
rows.adult: In school, students work on their own while the teacher runs small groups and reads reports [1][8].
rows.reports: A weekly dashboard, skills reports, school and district reports, and benchmark tests on the Quantile scale [7][8].
rows.evidence: Two correlational studies it commissioned, measured on its own test [9][10]. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating [12].

theirs: Happy Numbers is a PreK to grade 5 math program from Happy Numbers Inc. [1]. It presents itself as a math curriculum delivered through technology, so students can work on their own while the teacher runs small groups [1]. In the company's own kindergarten case study, a school used it beside its core program [16].

A student begins with a required placement test: adaptive, multiple choice and untimed. It sets a starting point on the Quantile scale [6][7]. Then the student works through curriculum tasks. In PreK these are tapping and dragging activities with voice prompts, and in grade 3 tasks build from objects and tape diagrams to arrays and equations [3][5]. Teachers set goals in minutes and tasks, and benchmark tests check progress during the year [2][8].
credit: Hands-on early math: tapping and dragging objects with voice prompts, and in kindergarten a sound feature for children who do not read yet [3][4].
Tasks move from objects and diagrams to symbols, so a picture comes before an equation [5].
Fact-fluency practice and game-style activities in the grade 3 pages [5].

theirs: Happy Numbers' main studies are two reports by LearnPlatform by Instructure, commissioned by Happy Numbers [9][10]. The first followed 540 kindergarten and grade 1 students in 30 schools of one midwestern district in 2021-22. It compared students by how many tasks they solved, controlling for fall scores. There was no group of non-users. Students with high use scored above students with low use by 0.45 standard deviations in kindergarten and 0.56 in grade 1 [9].

The second followed 1,590 students in grades 2 to 5 in two midwestern districts in 2022-23. Each extra 10 tasks went with 2.3 to 6.0 more points on the end-of-year test, depending on grade [10]. Both studies scored students on Happy Numbers' own test, which the first report calls "non-independent" [9]. A 2023-24 company brief on more than 113,000 students found heavier use went with more growth on its own scale, with no comparison group [11].

Happy Numbers calls the two LearnPlatform reports ESSA Tier III [2]. Evidence for ESSA lists Happy Numbers without a rating ("No studies met inclusion requirements") [12], and the What Works Clearinghouse has no intervention report on it [13]. We found no randomized trial of Happy Numbers.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% on the researchers' test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve mathematics performance [15]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is in PreK and you want tapping and dragging tasks with voice prompts.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no placement or benchmark tests.
You want help at every problem, and helped answers kept apart from what counts as learned.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past grade 5.
You want workbooks made from your child's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Happy Numbers?
questions.answer: Happy Numbers starts with a placement test, then a student works through curriculum tasks toward goals set in minutes and tasks [6][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Happy Numbers work?
questions.answer: Two studies the company commissioned from LearnPlatform found that students who solved more tasks scored higher on Happy Numbers' own test [9][10]. Both compared students by how much they used it. Evidence for ESSA lists it without a rating [12], and we found no randomized trial.

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs, and AMP places a learner from their first answers whatever else the learner uses.
